commonMistakes: Hips sagging so the body bends at the waist
Shrugging the shoulders up toward the ears
Using momentum instead of a controlled pull
cues: Pull your chest to the bar, elbows driving back
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top
Keep your body rigid — no sagging, no piking
instructions: Set a bar (or suspension-trainer handles) at about waist height. Lie underneath it and grip the bar with hands slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Walk your feet forward until your body hangs in a straight line, heels on the floor. The steeper your body angle, the harder the rep.
Pull your chest to the bar, driving your elbows back and squeezing your shoulder blades together.
Lower under control to straight arms. Keep your glutes braced so your body stays a rigid plank throughout.
longevityNotes: Pulling strength balances all the pushing and sitting of modern life, and it's the foundation of a healthy upper back and posture. The inverted row is the most joint-friendly way to build it — your feet stay on the ground, so you can scale the difficulty precisely and train the pulling pattern for decades without beating up your shoulders. Strong lats and rhomboids are what keep you upright at 80.
name: Inverted Row

progression.loadingGuidance: Lower the bar (steeper body angle) when you can do 3 sets of 12 with a 1-second pause at the top.
progression.regressTo: Standing band row at chest height

safetyNotes: Make sure the bar or anchor is secure before loading your full body weight. If you have an acute shoulder injury, keep the range pain-free and avoid the bottom stretch position.
